section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department diplomatic despatches, military intelligence reports, cross-reference sheets, and press clippings from 1931 to 1935 concerning political, social, and military conditions in Japanese-ruled Taiwan (Formosa). Key topics include the immediate political fallout of the 1930 Musha uprising, the subsequent April 1931 Second Musha massacre of protected tribesmen by Japanese-armed rivals, the police suppression of the Taiwan Minshuto political party, and persistent aboriginal unrest linked to land policies. The documents also address the domestic impact of the 1931–1932 Sino-Japanese conflict and refugee influxes, deliberations of the 1934 Local Governors Conference on assimilation and crop control, anti-American sentiment in the local press over naval talks, and a comprehensive 1935 reconnaissance report by the U.S. Military Attaché detailing Formosa's geography, transportation infrastructure, and military fortifications.

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 131 reporting on the causes of the Musha uprising and the resulting resignations of Formosan colonial officials.
subfiles.summary: According to a statement issued by the Government General of Formosa, the major cause of the aboriginal revolt at Musha in November 1930 was the requisitioning of native labor to transport timber for a new school, combined with resentment over family members executed for headhunting. Governor-General Ishidzuka and Vice Governor-General Hitomi resigned due to their responsibility for the uprising following conferences with Premier Hamaguchi and Foreign Minister Shidehara. In the Japanese Diet, the opposition sharply attacked the administration, questioning Overseas Affairs Minister Matsuda in particular. Kwantung Governor Ota was appointed as Ishidzuka's successor, an unpopular choice in Formosa though welcomed in Kwantung.
subfiles.title: The Revolt in Formosa: Statement of the Governor General of Formosa (Despatch No. 131 Extract)

subfiles.about: A confidential consular despatch reporting the forced dissolution of the Taiwan Minshuto political party under the Peace Preservation Law by Japanese authorities.
subfiles.summary: On February 18, 1931, the Taiwan Minshuto (Taiwan Democratic Party) convened a general meeting to adopt a platform advocating political freedom for laborers, self-government for adults over 18, abolition of the government opium monopoly, and reform of the Advisory Council. Following the session, Kita Police ordered the party dissolved under the Peace Preservation Law and arrested nineteen leading members on suspicions of communist affiliation. Vice Consul Reed reports that while authorities alleged radical tendencies, the true motives were government retaliation against the party's relentless campaigning against the profitable opium monopoly and its public critiques of the Musha affair. The despatch also details local cynicism surrounding official self-government commemorations and noted substantial increases in Persian opium imports used for illicit governmental revenue.
subfiles.title: Dissolution of the Taiwan Minshuto (Taiwan Democratic Party) (Despatch No. 71)

subfiles.about: A confidential consular despatch regarding reports and official denials of an aboriginal uprising near Heito, driven by fears of Japanese land confiscation.
subfiles.summary: Rumors emerged that aborigines from a village near Heito in Takao Prefecture attacked police patrols over apprehensions that their ancestral foothill lands were being confiscated. Although the Taiwan Government General, Takao Government, and Heito County Office issued categorical denials, defensive preparations were instituted and high police officials were dispatched to the scene. The unrest stemmed from the arrival of Japanese surveyors and widespread fears among mountain tribes of being forcibly relocated to unhealthy lowlands where they could not earn a livelihood. The despatch observes that Formosan Chinese shared this deep resentment against Japanese land policy, citing the Kanan Irrigation Project as an exploitative scheme designed to enrich Japanese officials and large landowners.
subfiles.title: Reported Uprising of Savages in Taiwan (Despatch No. 75)

subfiles.about: A confidential consular despatch reporting the Second Musha Incident, wherein Japanese-armed allied tribes massacred defenseless protected aborigines.
subfiles.summary: On April 25, 1931, armed members of the allied Tatsua tribe launched coordinated surprise raids against the defenseless villages of Rodof and Seepow, slaughtering nearly 200 members of the protected tribes who had been disarmed following the 1930 Musha uprising. Japanese police had ignored long-standing indications of an impending attack and permitted the Tatsua to retain rifles and ammunition while keeping the target tribes segregated and unarmed. The massacre was seen as serving the convenience of authorities by substantially reducing the number of aborigines requiring forced deportation, prompting cynical press remarks that emigration was made easy. The atrocity created serious political vulnerability for the central and prefectural administrations and caused financial nervousness regarding foreign loans for the Lake Candidius hydroelectric project.
subfiles.title: Massacre of Savages in Taiwan (Despatch No. 86)

subfiles.about: A confidential consular despatch reviewing police negligence in the Second Musha massacre and transmitting a critical editorial from the Japan Chronicle.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul Reed provides supplementary details on the Second Musha massacre, identifying the Togan tribe as an allied group and dismissing police assertions that the alleged decapitation of three Togan women justified the subsequent slaughter. Japanese authorities granted the Tatsua tribe days of grace when ordering the surrender of their firearms, affording the raiders sufficient time to execute the attack unhindered by police intervention. Tatsua leaders received only mild rebukes at the local police station and surrendered a portion of the decapitated heads, while the Department of Overseas Affairs minimized the incident as internal tribal warfare requiring no further action. An attached editorial from the Japan Chronicle severely criticizes the colonial government for gross negligence, double standards in tribal armament, and failed civilizing policies.
subfiles.title: Disturbances in the Savage Regions of Taiwan (Despatch No. 88 with Enclosure)

subfiles.about: A military intelligence report detailing an attack by Atayal aborigines on a Japanese police station at Pisian in Taichu Province.
subfiles.summary: On August 15, 1931, a band of aborigines raided the Japanese police post at Pisian, Tosai-gun, Taichu Province, killing five Japanese (including three police officers, two women, and a child) and capturing seven others while police were supervising road repairs. The attackers belonged to the Kayo tribe of the Taiyal (Atayal) group, who had secured a rifle and ammunition from local police under the pretext of hunting. Although 150 police reinforcements were dispatched, the rugged terrain prevented the capture of the perpetrators, forcing authorities to settle for a promise of good order from the tribal chieftain. The report notes that repeated Japanese military punitive expeditions have failed to subjugate the ferocious Taiyal tribes, who maintain deep contempt for Japanese authority.
subfiles.title: Formosan Aborigines Attack Police (Military Intelligence Report No. 5974)

subfiles.about: A State Department Document File Note referencing a report on Chinese resident anxiety in Taiwan and assistance provided to refugees from Foochow.
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references document 795.94/4059, originating from American Consul John B. Ketcham in Taihoku and dated February 8, 1932. The underlying report addresses unease among Chinese residents in Taiwan arising from the Sino-Japanese conflict in mainland China. It also records that the Government General of Taiwan was extending relief and assistance to refugees arriving from Foochow.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 795.94/4059

subfiles.about: A consular despatch detailing local reactions in Taiwan to the Shanghai Incident and the evacuation of refugees from Foochow.
subfiles.summary: Hostilities in Manchuria and fighting in Shanghai produced considerable tension among the 40,000 Chinese residents in Taiwan, leading the Chinese Consul General to issue instructions urging quiet neutrality and facilitating repatriation. On February 3, police detained forty Chinese residents for allegedly circulating rumors of Chinese military victories broadcast from Nanking. That same day, the steamer Choan Maru arrived at Keelung with 328 refugees from Foochow, consisting of Japanese nationals and Formosan Chinese subjects. Consul Ketcham also provides intelligence on Taiwan's garrison strength, estimating 8,000 troops concentrated in Taihoku and Tainan, alongside heavy coastal artillery installations at Keelung and the Pescadores Islands.
subfiles.title: Repercussions of the Sino-Japanese Situation in Taiwan (Despatch)

subfiles.about: A comprehensive consular despatch transmitting proceedings, policy directives, and local reports from the 1934 Taiwan Local Governors Conference.
subfiles.summary: From April 23 to 25, 1934, the annual conference of provincial and prefectural governors convened in Taihoku, opened by Governor-General Nakagawa and presided over by Director General of Administration Hiratsuka. Central administrative directives emphasized cultivating Japanese national spirit, worshipping Imperial shrines, aggressively propagating the Japanese language (currently understood by only 20% of Formosans), abolishing private Chinese schools (shobo), tightening police discipline, and enforcing rice crop diversification to curb exports to Japan. Five extensive enclosures summarize official addresses and reports from the governors of Taihoku, Shinchiku, Taichu, Tainan, Takao, Taito, Karenko, and Hoko covering agriculture, mining, harbor development, and aboriginal resettlement. Press commentary characterized the proceedings as routine and stereotyped, noting that governors deliberately avoided sensitive discussions of local self-government.
subfiles.title: Conference of Local Governors in Taiwan (Despatch with Enclosures 1-5)

subfiles.about: A consular despatch examining increasing anti-American bias in the local semi-official press regarding naval disarmament talks and Pacific diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul McConaughy reports a noticeable anti-American tone in the semi-official Taiwan Nichi Nichi, Formosa's most influential newspaper, which strongly molded local public opinion among Japanese and Formosan Chinese. This media hostility was stimulated by Japanese frustration over prolonged London naval conversations and outrage following public statements by a retired U.S. Army officer concerning Japan's aerial vulnerability. Three enclosed press translations reflect these themes: alleging American maneuvers to isolate Japan and disrupt Anglo-Japanese cooperation, interpreting U.S. Ambassador William C. Bullitt's visit to Nanking as an effort to negotiate a secret U.S.-Soviet-Chinese tripartite coalition, and examining British Dominion anxieties regarding closer Anglo-Japanese relations.
subfiles.title: Publishing of Political News Items in Local Press (Despatch with Enclosures 1-3)

subfiles.about: A military intelligence travel report detailing a reconnaissance tour of Taiwan covering transport networks, aboriginal populations, and military defenses.
subfiles.summary: Following the Japanese War Office's refusal to permit formal inspections of Taiwan Army units, Major Crane conducted an extensive ten-day reconnaissance tour of Taiwan in March 1935, traveling via railway, automobile, pushcar tram (daisha), and foot trails across the island. The report delivers an exhaustive technical assessment of Formosa's topography, road systems, pushcar tramways, coastal cliffs, and harbor capabilities at Keelung, Takao, Tansui, and Anping, while noting constant surveillance by Japanese military and civilian police. Major Crane describes the contrasting characteristics of aboriginal tribes, noting that foreign residents attributed the 1930 Musha massacre to police misconduct and the appropriation of native women. Taiwan Army Commander General Juichi Terauchi confirmed the garrison's composition of two infantry regiments, one mountain artillery battalion, one aviation regiment, and concealed coastal defense artillery at Keelung, Takao, and the Pescadores.
subfiles.title: Travel in Taiwan (Formosa) (Military Intelligence Report No. 7836)
subfiles.to: Chief, Military Intelligence Division, War Department
